I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked

Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I feel like I don't know myself anymore

vignette: Sara, a 69-year-old Middle Eastern woman, has been married for over forty years and works at a local fast food restaurant. Her life took an alarming turn several months ago when she became the victim of a relentless stalker who lurked outside her home and workplace. The trauma from this experience has deeply affected Sara’s daily functioning. At night, Sara often wakes up to check if everything is secure, convinced that someone might be out there watching or waiting for an opportunity to intrude. This constant vigilance has made it difficult for her to sleep soundly. Her husband has noticed how she scrutinizes the faces of everyone they encounter, looking for signs of potential danger. This hyper-vigilant behavior has extended beyond their home; even at work, Sara repeatedly checks that doors and windows are locked. The memory of the stalker lingering outside her house is vivid but strangely detached. Sometimes when Sara thinks about those terrifying moments, she can smell the scent of damp grass or gasoline from his car, which brings back a visceral sense of fear. Other times, she recalls the event with no emotional attachment at all; it feels as if someone else experienced these frightening episodes. Sara has come to believe that thinking about this traumatic experience is too overwhelming and would be unbearable to handle. This avoidance has led her to feel like an entirely different person—someone who cannot trust others or even recognize herself anymore. She now views people with suspicion, certain that they can’t be trusted after the betrayal she experienced. Her mistrust and fear have fueled a cycle of increasing anxiety and hypervigilance. Sara is constantly scanning her surroundings for any signs of danger, which only reinforces her negative beliefs about the world and others’ intentions. The more she feels threatened, the stronger her negative appraisals become, leading to an almost paranoid state where she questions everyone’s motives. Sara's husband has noticed a significant change in her behavior over the past few months. She is distant at home and often preoccupied with thoughts of safety and threat. At work, Sara finds herself frequently distracted by her need to check locks and assess potential threats, which has affected her performance and interactions with coworkers. Her manager has expressed concern about her declining focus and increased absences. The traumatic experience has left Sara feeling isolated and uncertain about who she can trust. The memory of the stalker's presence is so vivid that it feels surreal—like something out of a nightmare rather than reality. This detachment has only exacerbated her fear that she will not be able to cope if she fully confronts these memories. What finally brought Sara to seek help was her increasing isolation and her husband’s growing concern about her well-being. She is most afraid of becoming too overwhelmed by the past, but she hopes that with professional support, she can regain a sense of control and trust in herself and others.
